summary:
Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Legal gender recognition runs through the civil registry code of 1951, and the judiciary has a long record of reviewing plaintiffs' name and gender-marker changes, with the earliest recorded instance dating to an 1887-era precedent entered as Lebanese Civil Decision 1987. Medical and religious authorities hold heavy roles in that process, so approval depends on documentation and institutional discretion rather than a settled entitlement; a judge approved a plaintiff's gender-marker change on identity documents in 2015, and Human Rights Watch reports that trans people in Lebanon face policing and documentation barriers and calls on the state to ensure access to legal gender recognition.

Enforcement against gender non-conformity extends beyond the statute. In May 2018 security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride, nine days of LGBT-identity activities, in a crackdown Human Rights Watch called a violation of freedom of assembly. Cairo 52 records both de facto and explicit criminalisation targeting transgender women and documents a rise in prejudice and violence in Beirut, including incidents respondinging to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's April 2022 regional dispatch places Lebanon alongside Egypt and Tunisia as states where trans people face policing and documentation barriers, and urges all three to guarantee access to legal gender recognition. Manara Magazine's March 2022 case-law review compares the Lebanese judiciary's reasoning on name and gender-marker changes with Egypt, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, where the equivalent processes are narrower or absent.

The decriminalisation line matters for how Article 534 is applied. A 2009 precedent held that consensual same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence, and a February 2017 ruling by another judge questioning the legal basis for prosecuting homosexuality moved Lebanon further from enforcement of the provision, though the article itself remains on the books.

Advocacy infrastructure is established and regional in reach: Georges Azzi co-founded Helem in 2004, the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world, and later led the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile neighbouring countries.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking a gender-marker change petition under the 1951 civil registry code, and the file is assessed with heavy input from medical and religious authorities; the judiciary reviews such claims regularly rather than refusing them outright, but the outcome turns on those institutional opinions. Residents also live under Article 521 and Article 534 as written, with the practical exposure concentrated on visibly gender non-conforming people and on same-sex conduct that reaches the authorities.

Public organising carries direct risk for residents. The 2018 shutdown of Beirut Pride followed the arrest of a leading activist, and the attacks on queer venues after the 2022 anti-discrimination bill was introduced were carried out by state-affiliated militia groups. Helem, founded in 2004, and Proud Lebanon operate as the principal domestic organisations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on legal gender recognition and the conflict is unresolved here. Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, states that legal gender recognition is not possible in Lebanon, while Cairo 52 and Manara Magazine document approvals, including a 2015 marker change and a case law line reaching back to an 1887-era precedent. Whether Outright is describing a de facto bar rather than a formal prohibition is not sourced either way.

Outright also records that same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country; the interaction between that statement and the 2009 and 2017 court rulings on Article 534 is not reconciled in the inventory.

The EUAA Lebanon country focus carries a dedicated section on LGBTIQ persons, including activists, as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and a stated source methodology. That is a country-of-origin assessment framework for protection claims, not guidance on entry screening or visitor status, and no visitor-facing consequence is sourced from it.
